newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia reveals native title plans.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia reveals native title plans.

text.p: The Australian government on Tuesday revealed proposed amendments to the Native Title Act, under which it would become more difficult for aboriginal groups to force negotiations on land claims.
The government member charged with revamping the Native Title Act, Nick Minchin, said the amendments, contained in a discussion paper, would improve the workability of the bill.

The changes also represented the second stage of the government's election commitment to amend the act, Minchin, who is parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said in a statement. He said the latest amendments would:
-- Make it clear that the right to negotiate provisions would occur at the same time as state governments were processing applications for mining permits;
-- Improve the process for excluding activities such as exploration and prospecting from the negotiation process; and
-- Provide for more specific criteria to be followed by the arbitrators determining whether aborigines had native title to the land they claim;
-- Allow for earlier ministerial intervention in exceptional cases.
The amendments also set up a statutory framework for representative aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups, which would help to streamline the land claim process.
"The amendments include a voluntary agreement process which will provide greater flexibility to both indigenous and industry groups," Minchin said.
"They also introduce refinements to the new registration test, which are aimed at reducing the likelihood of multiple registered claims over one area," he said.
The Native Title Act, passed by the former Labor government, allows aboriginal groups to claim title on some traditional lands.
Miners and farmers have lobbied the new conservative Liberal-National government to alter the legislation, saying it was preventing or delaying mining and other projects from going ahead.
Minchin said the amendments contained in the discussion paper followed extensive consultation with various industry groups around Australia during July and August.
The amendment bill was introduced to the lower house of parliament in June, but has not been debated. Debate is due to start next week, a spokeswoman for Minchin said.
Minchin said the latest amendments would be introduced to parliament when the bill reached the upper house Senate. It is scheduled for debate there in early December.
Prime Minister John Howard has been promising changes to the legislation since the Liberal-National coalition won government on March 2.
